text: Backpropagation multiplies local derivatives along every path from the loss back to a weight, and in a deep network those paths are long. A long product is a fragile thing. Multiply many numbers that are a little smaller than one and the result shrinks towards zero; multiply many that are a little larger and it explodes. For years deep networks were notoriously hard to train, and this simple fact is a large part of the reason.

Consider a stack of sigmoid layers. The sigmoid's slope is never more than a quarter, so every layer the gradient passes through multiplies it by a quarter or less. After ten layers, the signal reaching the first layer is less than a millionth of what left the loss, so the early layers barely learn at all while the later ones do all the work. This is the vanishing gradient problem, and it hurts most where it matters, because the early layers build the features that everything else depends on.

The weights matter just as much as the activations. A layer adds up many inputs, each multiplied by a weight, and if the weights are too large the sum grows layer after layer, while if they are too small it shrinks. The same factor that scales the signal going forward also scales the gradient coming back, so a poor choice of starting weights can push a deep network into collapse or explosion before training has even begun.

The fix is to choose the spread of the random starting weights with care. When a neuron adds up n inputs, the variance of the sum grows in proportion to n, so drawing weights with a variance of one over n keeps the signal's size roughly constant from layer to layer. This is the idea behind Xavier initialisation, from Glorot and Bengio in 2010. For ReLU, which silences about half of its inputs, Kaiming He and colleagues showed in 2015 that the variance should be doubled, to two over n.

Why random at all, instead of starting every weight at the same sensible value? Because neurons that start identical stay identical. If every neuron in a layer has the same weights, each one computes the same output and receives exactly the same gradient, so after every update they are still clones, and the layer behaves like a single neuron however wide it is. Randomness breaks this symmetry and lets each neuron specialise.

Language models take this seriously. GPT-2, for instance, scales down the initial weights of the layers that write into each block's residual path, by one over the square root of their number, so that the signal does not grow as dozens of blocks add to it. Good initialisation is one of several defences, and the others, normalisation and residual connections, are coming up soon.

So the starting weights must be random, to break symmetry, and scaled to the size of each layer, so that signals neither fade nor explode. Next we look at normalisation, which keeps those signals in range throughout training, not just at the start.
